vignette:
Boon-Nam is a 72-year-old Cambodian-American man who works as a nanny for a family in suburban Maryland, caring for two young children during the day while his wife manages their small household nearby. He presented for psychological assessment following a referral from his primary care physician, who had grown concerned about his persistent sleep disturbance and what Boon-Nam described, with considerable reluctance, as feeling "never at peace." The events that brought him to this point stretch back nearly two years, though the wounds they left have not faded with time.

The abuse began gradually and then, one evening, became catastrophic. His partner at the time - a relationship he has since left - struck him repeatedly in a darkened room, and what Boon-Nam remembers most viscerally is the quality of that darkness: the way it erased the space around him, the way the blows came from directions he could not anticipate, and the way his body folded and braced against the floor. He eventually separated from that partner and, some months later, entered his current marriage. Yet the past did not stay where he placed it.

The memories themselves carry a strange, dissociated quality. Boon-Nam describes them as feeling like something that happened to another man - as though he is watching footage of a stranger - and yet when a memory surfaces, the terror is entirely his own, immediate and total. More disturbing still, his body participates: he finds himself physically contracting, shoulders rounding, arms drawing inward, recreating the posture of that night on the floor. These intrusive bodily reenactments are not passive recollections; they arrive with the full physiological force of the original event, and it is precisely because of this that Boon-Nam has constructed an elaborate architecture of avoidance around them. He suppresses any trace of anger - never allowing himself to feel it, let alone express it - because he has come to believe that emotional arousal of any kind is a threshold he cannot safely cross. He avoids darkness wherever possible, and he steers away from anything he judges potentially stressful, reasoning that if he can keep the conditions of his life sufficiently calm and featureless, the memories will have less to grip.

This vigilance, however, has not brought the peace he sought. His body remains in a state of chronic readiness. He startles at unexpected movement - a child darting suddenly across the room in the family's home where he works, a toy knocked from a shelf - and each time he reacts as though danger has arrived. He cannot relax even in his own living room, even when his wife is beside him and every rational faculty tells him he is safe. This persistent state of threat monitoring feeds directly back into the memories he is trying to contain: the hyperarousal keeps the nervous system primed, and in that primed state the intrusive recollections find easier purchase, surfacing with greater frequency and intensity. The loop tightens. Because the memories arrive so violently - with bodily reenactment, with full-spectrum terror - Boon-Nam redoubles his suppressive efforts, clamping down more firmly on emotional expression and withdrawing further from any circumstance that carries even a faint resemblance to that night. The darkness avoidance means he cannot accompany the children he cares for to certain rooms in the evening, a limitation he has quietly managed by reorganising the family's routine without explanation, though he worries the parents have begun to notice.

The avoidance strategies, meant to keep the memories at bay, have paradoxically preserved them. By never allowing the emotional material to be processed - by suppressing anger, by eliminating the triggers that might permit gradual desensitisation - Boon-Nam has kept the memories sealed in their original, unmetabolised form, ready to return with undiminished force whenever the perimeter he maintains is breached.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when one of the children stumbled and fell against him unexpectedly, and he grabbed the child's arm with a force that frightened them both. He sat in the car afterward and wept. What he most fears is that he is dangerous. What he most hopes is that someone can explain why, after all this time, it still feels like it is happening now.
